title: The diamond sent away
hook: the Koh-i-Noor is taken from the boy king and sent to Queen Victoria

segments.voice: Yesterday, bandhan, and your line was the kingdom ended. What ending did you sit with? Today, a stone that stood for that kingdom leaves it. Day nine hundred forty.

A small box, and inside it a single great diamond. Ranjit Singh wore it on his arm at court. Before him, Afghan rulers had held it, and Mughal emperors before them. Its name, the Koh-i-Noor, is usually given in English as the mountain of light. When the Punjab was annexed, the terms said this stone would go to the Queen of England. And it was taken from a boy who was still a child. Today: the diamond sent away.
screen: `A STONE IN A SMALL BOX.` → `WORN ON A MAHARAJA'S ARM.` → `THE MOUNTAIN OF LIGHT.`

segments.voice: First, the stone. The Koh-i-Noor had passed from ruler to ruler, often by force. Ranjit Singh obtained it from an Afghan king, Shah Shuja, who had come to him as a refugee, and the circumstances are still argued over. At Lahore it became a sign of the kingdom itself. Second, the terms. When Lord Dalhousie annexed the Punjab, the agreement named the Koh-i-Noor and said it was to be surrendered to the Queen. Dalhousie wanted it sent as a prize of the war, not as a gift from the Maharaja. Third, the journey. A story is told in the life of John Lawrence, one of the officers then governing the Punjab, that the stone was handed to him in its little box and he slipped it into a pocket and forgot it, until he was asked for it and had a bad moment searching. Then it was carried under guard to the coast and shipped to Britain. Fourth, what remains. In Britain the stone was cut down to a new shape, and it became part of the crown jewels. Its return has been asked for, from more than one country, and the question is still open. In Sikh tellings of this history, the diamond isn't really about wealth. It's about a child who lost his kingdom and then lost the sign of it too. Guru Nanak, in a hymn of the Guru Granth Sahib that tradition links to the invasion of Babur, says that for the sake of wealth, many were ruined and disgraced; it can't be gathered without wrongdoing, and it doesn't go with you when you die. That's today's line.
screen: `A STONE THAT PASSED FROM HAND TO HAND.` · `NAMED IN THE TERMS.` · `A BOX IN A POCKET, THEN A SHIP.` · `WHAT WEALTH CANNOT CARRY.` · then, large: `TAKEN AWAY.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with open hands. Sit, and rest your hands palm up on your knees. Bring to mind one thing you hold onto tightly: an object, a role, a picture of how things should be. Notice whether your hands want to close around it. Now, on each breath out, let the fingers soften a little. You aren't giving anything away. You're only noticing that your hands can be open while the thing is still yours. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Moh, attachment, the grip that won't open, the Gurus warn: the Koh-i-Noor, worn by Ranjit Singh, taken from his son for the Queen. Today's word.
Your line: taken away. Today, let go of one small precious thing, a grudge, a plan, an object, and notice what's left in your open hand. Day nine hundred forty.

howItsDone: The Koh-i-Noor remains in the British crown jewels, and in Sikh tellings of the annexation it stands for everything taken from Maharaja Duleep Singh as a child.

notes: The meaning of the name Koh-i-Noor (mountain of light) is given without an etymology; confirm.
Koh-i-Noor's chain of owners (Mughal, Afghan, Shah Shuja to Ranjit Singh) and 'circumstances still argued over' should be checked.
Dalhousie's insistence that it be a prize of war, not a gift: confirm against his letters or a standard history.
The pocket story is from Bosworth Smith's Life of Lord Lawrence; told as a story. Confirm.
'Its return has been asked for, from more than one country' — confirm wording.
Babarvani (is jar kaaran ghanee vigutee...) paraphrased; confirm Ang 417 and the lines about wealth not going with you.
